biomimicry-creative-problem-solving.title: Translate a Problem into a Nature-Inspired Design Principle
biomimicry-creative-problem-solving.description: Describe the function a solution must perform, inspect a biological example, extract a transferable principle and test one safe application without copying the organism literally.
biomimicry-creative-problem-solving.reason: Replace fabricated capacity, cleaning, communication and team outcomes with a bounded function-to-principle design exercise.
forbidden_public_fragments: Our own count last month: 43 models considered
Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Translate a design problem into a function, inspect how a biological system performs a similar function and extract one principle to test safely.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State what the solution must do without naming the current solution. Choose a biological example from a reliable description. Separate the observed structure or process from the metaphor. Write one transferable principle, generate several applications and test the smallest reversible option within safety and operational constraints.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What function did I study, what principle did I extract, and what did the small test reveal about its usefulness or limit?

faq.question: Is a nature metaphor enough?
faq.answer: No. State the function and the observable structure or process. A poetic comparison can inspire ideas, but it is not yet a design principle.

faq.question: Should I copy the biological form directly?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Scale, material, environment and purpose can differ. Extract a principle and test an application suited to your constraints.

faq.question: What if the biological description is uncertain?
faq.answer: Use a better documented example or label the idea as a loose analogy and test only the design concept.

intro.html: Nature-inspired design becomes useful when the problem is translated into a function and the biological example is inspected for a transferable principle.

sections.title: 1. Define the function
sections.html: Describe what the solution must do: route, filter, attach, cool, distribute, protect, adapt or recover. Remove the current solution from the sentence.

sections.title: 2. Choose an example and extract the principle
sections.html: Find a reliable description of a biological system performing a similar function. Write the relevant structure or process in neutral terms and separate it from the organism's name.

sections.title: 3. Generate applications and test one
sections.html: Apply the principle to your materials, workflow or layout. Keep several options, then choose a reversible prototype that respects safety, welfare and operational constraints.

bold-brainstorm-kickoff.title: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality
bold-brainstorm-kickoff.description: Start an idea session with a deliberately unrealistic seed, explore its consequences without defending it and then translate useful fragments back into real constraints.
bold-brainstorm-kickoff.reason: Replace fabricated session logs, keeper multipliers, percentage outcomes and tested-duration claims with a bounded provocation-to-feasible-idea exercise.

lifeOsSource.hack: Begin with one deliberately extreme assumption, explore what it changes and then keep only the fragments that survive real constraints.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the real problem. Choose an extreme seed that changes one constraint, customer, resource or rule. During a short generation round, list consequences and variants without arguing with the seed. Remove the seed, restore actual constraints and choose one feasible fragment to test or develop.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which useful fragment came from the extreme seed, and what real constraint or next test made it actionable?

faq.question: Does the bold seed need to be realistic?
faq.answer: No. It is a temporary lens, not a proposal. The final idea must still pass the real constraints after the seed is removed.

faq.question: What if the group starts debating the seed?
faq.answer: Remind everyone that evaluation comes later. Write consequences and variants first, then return to feasibility in a separate pass.

faq.question: Are all extreme prompts acceptable?
faq.answer: No. Avoid prompts that normalize harm, broken consent or unsafe shortcuts. Boldness does not remove boundaries.

intro.html: An unrealistic seed can move a session away from the first familiar answer. Its purpose is temporary: expose consequences and variants, then remove the seed and select only what remains useful.

sections.title: 1. State the problem and choose a seed
sections.html: Write the outcome, audience and main constraint. Reverse one constraint, remove a resource, change the customer or imagine an unusual rule.

sections.title: 2. Explore without evaluation
sections.html: List what would change in behavior, sequence, ownership, cost, communication or failure. Do not argue with feasibility during this pass.

sections.title: 3. Restore constraints and choose one test
sections.html: Return to the real budget, time, safety and technical limits. Select one fragment that can be prototyped or checked and record what would make you discard it.
